summary: British Togoland was a West African territory administered by the United Kingdom, created in 1916 when the German protectorate of Togoland was split between Britain and France during the First World War. It began as a League of Nations Class B mandate, was formally placed under British rule in 1922, and after the Second World War became a United Nations Trust Territory still administered by the UK. A May 1956 plebiscite saw a majority of voters choose to merge the territory with the neighbouring Gold Coast.
one_line: A former West African territory under UK administration, split from German Togoland in 1916 and merged with the Gold Coast after a 1956 plebiscite.
key_facts: British Togoland was officially called the Mandate Territory of Togoland and later the Trust Territory of Togoland.
British Togoland was effectively formed in 1916 by splitting the German protectorate of Togoland into two territories.
The split that created British Togoland took place during the First World War.
Initially British Togoland was a League of Nations Class B mandate.
In 1922 British Togoland was formally placed under British rule.
In 1922 French Togoland, now Togo, was placed under French rule.
Following the Second World War, British Togoland became a United Nations Trust Territory.
British Togoland remained administered by the United Kingdom after becoming a United Nations Trust Territory.
A plebiscite was organised in British Togoland in May 1956 to decide the territory's future.
The plebiscite was held during the decolonization of Africa.
A majority of voters taking part in the May 1956 plebiscite voted to merge British Togoland with the neighbouring Gold Coast.
The Gold Coast was a British Crown colony at the time of the 1956 plebiscite.
